concept.body: Same recipe, different slice count: divide 360° by the number of vertices to get the central angle. Square → 360 ÷ 4 = 90°. Triangle → 360 ÷ 3 = 120°. Hexagon → 360 ÷ 6 = 60°. Equal slices force equal sides.

explanationVariants: An inscribed square divides the circle into 4 equal central angles: 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.
Four equally spaced vertices means four 90° slices.

widget.prompt: What is the central angle of an inscribed SQUARE, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 120° is the TRIANGLE's central angle (3 vertices). A square has 4: 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.
60° is the HEXAGON's (6 vertices). A square has 4: 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.

steps.body: The square comes from **perpendicular diameters**. Draw a diameter, construct its perpendicular through the center (a diameter too), and the four points where these cross the circle are the square's vertices — four equal 90° slices of the circle.

widget.prompt: Inscribe a square in a circle. Reveal each stage.

panels.title: Draw a diameter
panels.body: Draw any line through the center, meeting the circle at two opposite points.

panels.title: Perpendicular diameter
panels.body: Construct the perpendicular to that diameter through the center — it hits the circle at two more points.

panels.title: Four points
panels.body: The four crossing points are 90° apart around the circle.

panels.title: Connect them
panels.body: Join consecutive points: an inscribed square.

widget.continueFeedback: Reveal each step of crossing the diameters.
widget.successFeedback: Four points 90° apart — an inscribed square.

widget.prompt: The diameter's ends are 4 apart. Find the smallest whole radius whose arcs cross — the line through the crossings carries the square's other two vertices.
widget.successFeedback: Radius 3 — just past half of 4. The line through the crossings is perpendicular to the diameter AND passes through its midpoint, the circle's center — so it is the second diameter, and its circle-crossings complete the square. Equal central angles of 90° each: that is where “regular” comes from.
widget.lowFeedback: The two arcs each reach only their own radius; together they must beat the 4 between the ends — the radius has to clear 2.
widget.highFeedback: They cross, but not at the SMALLEST whole radius that manages it. Ease back down.

predict.prompt: AB is the circle's diameter. The construction bisects it with equal arcs. Where must the bisector's crossing points land?

options.label: On the circle — they become the square's other two vertices
Strictly inside the circle, near the center
Anywhere — it depends on the compass opening

predict.reveal: The perpendicular bisector of a diameter passes through the center, so it is itself a diameter line — and a diameter meets the circle at two points. Those two points, with A and B, are four circle points a quarter-turn apart: the inscribed square. The compass opening only decides where the ARCS cross; the line they fix was never in doubt.

explanationVariants: Four equally spaced vertices divide 360° into four parts: 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.
Perpendicular diameters cross at 90°, and those right angles ARE the central angles of the square.

widget.prompt: An inscribed square's four vertices divide the circle equally. What is each central angle, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 360° is the WHOLE turn. Split it among the four vertices: 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.
45° would be 360 ÷ 8 — an octagon's spacing. A square has 4 vertices: 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.

steps.body: The equilateral triangle uses **three 120° arcs**. One way: inscribe a hexagon and keep every other vertex. Another: from any circle point, an arc of the circle's radius marks two neighbors 60° away — the three alternate marks span 120° each and form the triangle.

widget.prompt: An inscribed equilateral triangle's three vertices divide the circle equally. What is each central angle, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 60° is the HEXAGON's central angle. The triangle uses every OTHER hexagon vertex, doubling to 360 ÷ 3 = 120°.
3 is the vertex count, not an angle. Each central slice is 360 ÷ 3 = 120°.

explanationVariants: The radius steps 6 times around (the hexagon). The equilateral triangle keeps every OTHER step, so it uses 3 of those 6 marks.
Six equal 60° arcs, taken two at a time (120° each), give the triangle's 3 vertices.

widget.prompt: Using the radius-stepping method, the compass makes 6 equally spaced marks. How many of them are the vertices of the inscribed equilateral TRIANGLE?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 marks make the HEXAGON. The triangle keeps every OTHER one: 3 vertices.
4 vertices make a square — and the square comes from perpendicular diameters, not the 6 radius-marks. The triangle uses 3 of the 6.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Every other of the 6 marks: 3 vertices.

steps.body: All three share one engine: **equal central angles make equal chords make a regular polygon**. Divide 360° into n equal slices and the n chords are forced equal, so the figure is regular. The compass just delivers the equal slices — 60° by radius-stepping, 90° by perpendicular diameters.

widget.prompt: Why do equal central angles guarantee a REGULAR polygon (all sides and angles equal)?

options.label: Equal central angles cut equal chords, giving equal sides and angles.
options.feedback: In one circle, equal central angles subtend equal chords — so every side matches, which is what "regular" means.

options.label: A compass automatically makes every side and angle equal.
options.feedback: The compass draws whatever length it's set to — the regularity comes from equal ANGLES forcing equal chords, not the tool.

options.label: Every polygon inscribed in a circle is automatically regular.
options.feedback: A lopsided inscribed quadrilateral is not regular. Regularity needs the vertices EQUALLY spaced — equal central angles.

options.label: Equal central angles force a larger polygon, not a regular one.
options.feedback: Size is set by the radius, not the angles. Equal angles make the polygon REGULAR, not larger.

hints: Match each polygon to how its equal central angle is produced.
60° comes from radius-stepping; 90° comes from a perpendicular.
The square's 90° slices come from perpendicular DIAMETERS through the center.
explanationVariants: The square's 90° central angles come from perpendicular diameters; the hexagon's 60° from radius-stepping; the triangle from taking every other hexagon mark.
Perpendicular diameters → 4 vertices at 90°. That's the square's signature move.

widget.prompt: Which inscribed polygon is built from two PERPENDICULAR diameters?

options.label: the square
options.feedback: Perpendicular diameters cross the circle at four points 90° apart — the square's vertices.

options.label: the hexagon
options.feedback: The hexagon comes from stepping the RADIUS around (60° arcs), not from perpendicular diameters.

options.label: the equilateral triangle
options.feedback: The triangle uses every other hexagon mark (120° arcs) — no perpendicular diameter is needed.

options.label: the regular pentagon
options.feedback: The pentagon needs 72° arcs, which neither radius-stepping nor perpendicular diameters produce directly.

takeaways: Equilateral triangle: every other hexagon mark → 3 vertices at 120°.
Equal central angles force equal chords — that's what makes each polygon regular.
